Learning Objectives
Describe the anatomy and biomechanics of phalangeal fractures, metacarpal fractures, and
dislocations.
Evaluate phalangeal and metacarpal injuries, including radiographic parameters and clinical
examination findings.
List treatment options for the management of phalangeal fractures, metacarpal fractures, and
dislocations, including indications for surgical management.

Fractures of the metacarpals and phalanges are among the most common fractures of the
upper extremities.1,2
Percentage of total hand fractures by location
Distal phalanx: 45% to 50%
Metacarpal: 30% to 35%
Proximal phalanx: 15% to 20%
Long phalanx: 8%
Mechanism of Injury
Distal phalanx fractures tend to be mallet fractures from an axial force or crushing injuries
creating a comminuted fracture.
The most common metacarpal fractures involve the little finger, and most result from
punching.
Spiral fractures usually reflect a torsional mechanism of injury.1
One of the most common proximal phalanx fractures is to the base of the little finger, usually
after a fall from a standing height.
Associated Injuries
Soft-Tissue Injuries
Skin: open fractures, dermal edema
Flexor tendons
Extensor tendons
Collateral ligaments
Neurovascular Injuries
With crush, laceration, avulsion
Digital nerve laceration versus neuropraxia

Physical Examination

Physical Examination
Note any rotational or angular deformities and wounds. Palpate for focal tenderness or
crepitation. Encourage active flexion to assess for rotational deformity. Other techniques
to assess rotational alignment include evaluating the cascade of the digits (they should
all approximately point to the scaphoid tubercle in flexion) and the rotational alignment
of the nails (the ring and little fingers may rotate slightly toward the long finger; Figure
1).
Figure 1 Photograph of the hand of a patient who sustained a spiral fourth metacarpal
shaft fracture shows rotational deformity of the ring finger and digital overlap.
(Reproduced from Geissler WB, Keen CA, Barber JA: Surgical fixation of metacarpal
fractures, in Colvin AC, Flatow E, eds: Atlas of Essential Orthopaedic Procedures, ed 2.

To assess joint stability, apply ulnar and radial stress with the joint in full extension and
in 30° of flexion. Assess the integrity of tendon insertions by testing the functions of each
tendon (eg, distal interphalangeal (DIP) flexion for the flexor digitorum profundus).
Patients usually can be put sufficiently at ease for an adequate physical examination.
The physical examination also can be repeated after a few days and even repeated via
video. In uncommon circumstances in which a prompt decision is necessary and the
physical examination is limited by pain, a digital block may alleviate pain to allow for a
more complete assessment of potential rotational deformity or ligamentous stability.
Neurovascular Examination

Neurovascular Examination
Assess digital perfusion and estimate ischemia time.3 Doppler ultrasonography can be
used to evaluate the integrity of the digital vessels or pulse oximetry can be used to
compare the injured digit to an uninjured digit. For potential nerve injuries, evaluate
gross two-point discrimination. In a patient with a mangling injury, exploration in the
operating room may be planned. If additional information is desired, pin prick of the
radial and ulnar sides of the hand is sufficient (Table 1).

Imaging Studies

Imaging Studies
Radiographs are the most common initial imaging study for all fractures or dislocations
in the hand. In evaluating fingers, ensure the radiograph is of the finger itself rather than
the hand. Evaluate for subtle changes, such as a V sign on lateral finger radiographs;
widening of the dorsal aspect of the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint is suggestive of
joint subluxation. In uncommon situations with articular comminution, a CT scan may be
helpful. Occasionally, MRI is considered for ligamentous injuries (eg, possible Stener
lesion of the thumb metacarpophalangeal [MCP] joint); however, most ligament
diagnoses can be made via physical examination alone.
General Treatment Principles
Nonsurgical Management
Metacarpal Fractures
Displaced fractures may benefit from closed reduction.
Most minimally displaced fractures can be managed with the use of a splint for comfort and to
allow motion.
Phalangeal Fractures

Surgical management often is considered for displaced fractures; however, many displaced
fractures (eg, angulated proximal phalanx base fractures) and minimally displaced fractures
with adequate alignment can be managed with the use of buddy straps and protected motion.
Immobilization always is 4 weeks or less.
Dislocation of Finger Joints
DIP, PIP, and MCP joints usually are stable after reduction of a complete dislocation and can be
managed via a short period of immobilization for comfort.
Motion and stretching are important to limit stiffness.
Buddy straps allow for comfort and motion.
Surgical Fracture Fixation
Hand Fractures
Treatment goals (all fractures)
Adequate length, angular and rotational alignment, and optimization of articular congruity
Repair of injured soft tissues
Enhancement of recovery via greater movement and use after fixation
Ability of a fracture to maintain alignment as it heals
Largely related to initial displacement
Fracture location, fracture morphology, bone quality, comminution, and soft-tissue injury
also are important considerations.
Considerations for fixation (Table 2)

in Wolfe S, Pederson W, Hotchkiss R, Kozin S, Cohen M, eds: Green’s Operative Hand Surgery, ed 7.
Philadelphia, PA, Elsevier, 2016, pp 239-290.
General principles of fixation
Biomechanics
More metal is stronger (common sense), but what is strong enough? And what are the
advantages and disadvantages of using more metal?
Screws are stronger than Kirschner wires (K-wires).
Plate and screw constructs may be stronger than screws alone.
Plate and screw constructs in the digits may be bulky and may be associated with more
tendon adhesions and stiffness.
Screws can be used without a plate if fracture length is at least twice the bone diameter.
Some surgeons prefer to avoid a gliding hole (interfragmentary compression screw)
because the cortices are so thin in the hand. Compression can be applied with the use of a
clamp rather than through a screw.
Selection of fixation method
Closed extra-articular fractures are managed via closed reduction and percutaneous pinning
(CRPP), if possible. This avoids surgical dissection with consequent scarring.
Open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) generally is reserved for fractures with
associated soft-tissue injury and unstable articular or non-articular fractures. The rationale is
that more rigid fixation allows for active motion to limit adhesions expected from these
injury aspects.
Open management also is used for partially healed fractures. Most hand fractures cannot be
reduced in a closed manner after approximately 7 to 10 days.

Intramedullary fixation is an alternative for some fractures, such as little finger metacarpal
shaft or neck fractures.
Specific Injuries
Metacarpal Fractures
Anatomy and Biomechanics
The hand can accommodate dorsal angulation by compensating with MCP joint
hyperextension and carpometacarpal (CMC) joint motion. The index and long CMCs are
immobile; the little finger has approximately 30° of motion, and the ring finger has
approximately 20° of motion, making them better able to accommodate angular deformity.
Rotational deformity of more than 5° may lead to overlapping of the fingers in flexion
(scissoring).
Angular deformity at the metacarpal neck/metaphysis influences tendon balance less than at
the diaphyseal level.
Cadaver experiments estimate 7° of extensor lag per 2 mm of metacarpal shortening;
however, compensation is variable. MCP joint hyperextension usually can compensate for as
much as 4 mm of shortening.4
Metacarpal shortening or angulation greater than 30° may result in shortening of the
intrinsics, with the potential for extensor lag at the PIP.
Metacarpal shaft fractures are inherently stable because of the connections at the CMC joints
and the intermetacarpal ligaments.
Metacarpal Head Fractures
Epidemiology: uncommon and usually intra-articular5
Radiography: PA, lateral, oblique, and Brewerton views
The Brewerton view aids in visualizing avulsion fractures and articular injuries. The view
involves flexing the MCP joint 40° to 65° with the dorsal hand placed on the image receptor
(Figure 2).

Figure 2 Brewerton radiograph of the metacarpal heads in a normal hand demonstrates
excellent visualization of the articular surface. (Reproduced from Geissler WB, Keen CA, Barber JA:
Surgical fixation of metacarpal fractures, in Colvin AC, Flatow E, eds: Atlas of Essential Orthopaedic

Management
Nonsurgical management
Minimally displaced
Collateral ligament avulsion
Surgical management may be considered depending on the stability of the joint and the
size of the avulsed fragment.
Surgical management
In most patients, a dorsal longitudinal approach is favored. The extensor tendon can be
split longitudinally, or the sagittal band can be split and the extensor tendon can be
retracted. The soft tissue needs to be repaired to prevent extensor lag or extensor tendon
subluxation.
Simple fractures can be managed via ORIF with the use of K-wires or screws.
Open injuries, including fight bite injuries with or without associated fractures, are
débrided and irrigated initially. If necessary, internal fixation can be performed during a
second or third surgical procedure after the wound is clean.

Comminuted fractures can be managed with the use of multiple K-wires, screws, cerclage
wires, or a plate and screws. Some may benefit from brief immobilization.
Some articular fractures are so fragmented (missing bone or articular fragments) that MCP
joint arthroplasty or arthrodesis may be considered; however, this decision can be made
after an initial examination, and management can be staged. In addition, surgeons may
wait for the results of less management and consider arthroplasty or arthrodesis later for
the management of arthritis or nonunion.
Complications: stiffness, arthritis, and rare osteonecrosis

Metacarpal Head Fractures
The MCP joint is a multiaxial condyloid joint that permits an arc of motion from 15° of
hyperextension to 110° of flexion.6 The center of rotation is not fixed because of the
eccentric attachments of the collateral ligaments. Fractures of the metacarpal head are
uncommon compared with other metacarpal fractures.
McElfresh and Dobyns7 described 10 separate fracture patterns of the metacarpal head.
The authors found the most commonly injured digit was the index metacarpal (40%),
and athletic injuries were the most common mechanism of injury, followed by direct
axial force (eg, punching). The fractures often were open (21%), and the most common
fracture pattern was comminuted (30%).7
Intra-articular impaction or shear fractures may block motion.8 The skin is evaluated for
lacerations, especially in patients with a strike injury because fight bites are at risk for
infection.
Radiographs of suspected metacarpal head fractures include standard PA, lateral, and
oblique views. A tangential Brewerton view, with the MCP joints flexed 65° and the x-ray
beam angled 15° ulnar to radial, is obtained for evaluation of suspected collateral
ligament injuries.9 In addition to radiographs, CT may be useful for surgical planning in
patients with complex fractures.

11/37

Nonsurgical management, with the MCP joint briefly immobilized in flexion, followed by
motion with the use of buddy straps for comfort, may be considered for minimally
displaced or collateral avulsion fractures.6 The articular surfaces of the MCP joint
remodel over time, and a functional joint can be achieved, even with some articular
incongruity.4 Displaced and/or unstable articular fractures are managed on a case-by-
case basis. Various surgical approaches have been described; however, a longitudinal
dorsal approach, splitting the extensor tendon or the sagittal band, is the preferred
approach. ORIF with the use of K-wires, screws, and plates has been described.6,7,10,11
The goal is fixation secure enough to begin moving the hand and fingers. For more
tenuous fixation, immobilization should be limited no more than 3 to 4 weeks postinjury
or postoperatively. MCP joint salvage options include arthrodesis and arthroplasty.6
Finger Metacarpal Neck Fractures
Epidemiology: common, usually involve ring and little finger metacarpals
Radiography: PA, lateral, and oblique views
Management
Nonsurgical management
Shortening less than 6 mm and rotation less than 5°12
Rotation is rare with metacarpal neck fractures.
Angular deformity is largely aesthetic; motion, function, and joint health are not affected.
With notable angular deformity, patients may feel the metacarpal head in their palm if they
grip an object.
Offer of surgical management
Surgical management
May be considered for angulation as much as 15° in the index finger, 20° in the long finger,
30° in the ring finger, and 40° to 50° in the little finger.12-14
Discretionary and largely aesthetic for the most common little finger metacarpal neck
fracture.12
Techniques include antegrade intramedullary pins; retrograde, trans-articular
intramedullary screw; transverse pinning; cross-pinning; or plate and screw fixation (Figure
3).
Complications: stiffness, extensor lag, loss of knuckle prominence


Finger Metacarpal Neck Fractures
Metacarpal neck fractures are common, usually involve the ring and little finger
metacarpals, and typically result from a clenched fist striking a solid object.5 Patients
present with pain and loss of knuckle contour and may have an extensor lag. The soft
tissue surrounding the MCP joint is evaluated for a fight bite, resulting in an MCP joint

9/3/26, 4:12 PM
AAOS | Fractures and Dislocations of the Hand and Digits
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001168
13/37

arthrotomy. This is managed via débridement, irrigation, and prophylactic antibiotic
agents. Workup includes standard PA, lateral, and oblique radiographs.
Metacarpal neck fractures tend to lose any realignment after closed reduction because
of volar comminution and pull from the intrinsics, which lie volar to the axis of the MCP
joint.15 Immobilization in MCP joint flexion is common to avoid collateral shortening.
Immobilization in extension has been described, resulting in adequate return of motion,
but affords no advantages in final fracture angulation.15 This also may aid in limiting an
initial MCP joint extension lag.
Surgical management may be offered if angulation is greater than 10° in the index, 20° in
the long, greater than 30° in the ring, and greater than 40° in the little finger
metacarpals. Greater angulation is permitted for metacarpal neck fractures of the ring
and little fingers because of increased CMC joint motion compared with the index and
long metacarpals.5 Rotation of a metacarpal neck fracture is exceedingly rare. Re-
evaluation is necessary if rotation is suspected. For the little finger metacarpal neck,
surgical management often is aesthetic (sunken knuckle) because deformity at the
metacarpal neck level does not affect tendon balance, motion, or strength; however,
patients may have a lump in palm sensation or painful callus with gripping because of
the volar prominence of the metacarpal head.
Most surgeons prefer less invasive techniques (CRPP) if performing surgical
stabilization.5 If open reduction is necessary, surgical stabilization may be performed
with the use of a plate-and-screw construct or pinning. Any open surgical procedure is
associated with a risk of stiffness, and tendon irritation may be heightened with the use
of a plate.
Finger Metacarpal Shaft Fractures
Epidemiology: common
Radiography: PA and lateral with or without oblique views (Figure 4)
Management
Nonsurgical management

Shortening less than 5 mm and rotation less than 5°12
Angular deformity of the metacarpal shaft is more noticeable and may affect finger tendon
balance more than deformity at the neck.
Surgical management
Surgical management often is offered for 10° of angulation at the index and long finger
metacarpals and 20° of angulation at the ring and little finger metacarpals.
Angulation and shortening are largely aesthetic; however, malrotation may affect
function.12
Open injuries, multiple displaced metacarpal fractures, and polytrauma
Techniques
Long oblique: lag screws
Transverse or short oblique: pinning, intramedullary fixation, plating
Multiple fractures: plating or intramedullary fixation
Complications: stiffness, extensor lag, malrotation, tendon imbalance (palmar displacement of
the metacarpal head resulting in hyperextension at the MCP joint)

Finger Metacarpal Shaft Fractures
Most metacarpal diaphyseal fractures have apex dorsal angulation because of the pull of
the interossei, which results in flexion of the distal fragment. Acceptable angulation is
less than that for metacarpal neck fractures because the deformity is thought to create
more tendon imbalance.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:12 PM
AAOS | Fractures and Dislocations of the Hand and Digits
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001168
16/37

Most metacarpal diaphyseal fractures do well without surgical management. Many
metacarpal shaft fractures are inherently stable, and immobilization is for comfort only.
Surgical management of diaphyseal metacarpal fractures is variable and may include
percutaneous K-wires placed transversely into the adjacent metacarpal or across the
fracture site, open screw or plate and screw fixation (usually applied dorsally), or
intramedullary screws/devices. Long oblique or spiral fractures can be secured with the
use of two or three screws. Short oblique or transverse fractures can be managed via
plate or intramedullary fixation. Retrograde, trans-articular intramedullary headless
screw fixation is an increasingly used treatment option associated with good clinical
outcomes and limited risks.16-19
In the management of metacarpal diaphyseal bone loss, fixation can restore length and
alignment, and autogenous bone graft can be applied, if necessary, immediately, with
limited contamination and good débridement, or after the wound is clean from
additional débridement procedures, soft-tissue coverage as necessary, and time.
Malunion of metacarpal fractures may be managed via opening or closing wedge
osteotomies or derotational osteotomies in combination with internal fixation.
Finger Metacarpal Base Fractures
Epidemiology
Index and long finger metacarpal base fractures: rare
Ring finger metacarpal base fractures: uncommon
Little finger metacarpal base fractures: common
Imaging studies
Radiographs: PA, lateral, and oblique views
CT scans: occasionally may be helpful in patients with a CMC joint fracture-dislocation in
which a carpal bone may be fractured or to assess articular alignment and fragmentation
Management
Fracture dislocations with large articular fragments are managed surgically.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:12 PM
AAOS | Fractures and Dislocations of the Hand and Digits
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001168
17/37

Non-articular fractures heal naturally, and deformity is largely aesthetic.
Closed reduction and pin fixation may be considered for widely displaced fractures.

Finger Metacarpal Base Fractures
Fractures of the metacarpal base usually are non-articular. Articular fractures may be
CMC joint fracture-dislocations. Fracture-dislocations of the CMC joint of the little and
ring fingers are displaced proximally and ulnarly because of the pull of the extensor
carpi ulnaris tendon. If a large articular fragment is present, surgical management may
be necessary to maintain joint alignment.
Oblique radiographs may help assess displacement (supinated oblique views). CT is
helpful if articular impaction, fracture-dislocation, or carpal fracture is suspected.
Compared with the index and long CMC joints, considerable motion occurs at the little
and ring finger CMC joints. Good joint alignment helps maintain mobility of the fourth
and fifth CMC joints. Fracture-dislocations with small marginal fractures (of the
metacarpal or carpus) and limited articular impaction may be managed via closed
reduction and immobilization/monitoring or via K-wire fixation if substantial concern for
re-dislocation exists. Larger fragments and impaction may benefit from ORIF20 and
possibly bone grafting. Very fragmented fractures may benefit from temporary external
fixation or bridging plate fixation.
Occasionally, patients will present with an undermanaged injury in the subacute setting.
Typically, if the duration from injury to potential surgical management is more than 4
weeks, then nonsurgical management is preferred. Symptomatic posttraumatic arthritis
is uncommon; therefore, such a diagnosis should be made with care. With careful
consideration and readiness, arthrodesis is a treatment option.
Thumb Metacarpal Fractures
Thumb Metacarpal Shaft/Epibasal Fractures
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:12 PM
AAOS | Fractures and Dislocations of the Hand and Digits
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001168
18/37

Epidemiology: epibasal fractures occurring at the proximal metaphyseal-diaphyseal junction
are common.5
Radiographs: AP, oblique, and true lateral views of the thumb
Management
Nonsurgical management
As much as 30° of angulation is acceptable because of the mobility of the saddle joint.
Monitor closely for displacement.
Surgical management
Usually managed via CRPP
Open reduction for partially healed fractures can be secured with the use of a plate and
screws.
Thumb Metacarpal Articular Base Fractures
Epidemiology: Fracture of the volar ulnar margin with dislocation of the joint (Bennett) is much
more common than a fragmented articular fracture of the entire base (Rolando).
Many Bennett fractures also have articular impaction.
Imaging studies
Hyperpronated AP (Robert) and true lateral views
Consider CT to evaluate joint for comminuted fractures.
Bennett fracture (Figure 5)
Pathoanatomy
The volar oblique ligament is attached to the volar ulnar fragment of the base.
The abductor pollicis longus displaces the distal metacarpal proximally, and the adductor
pollicis displaces the metacarpal into adduction.
The metacarpal base is displaced dorsally and rotated into supination.
Management
Nonsurgical management
Anatomic or near anatomic reduction and no articular impaction21
Nonsurgical management is rare because of inherent instability resulting from the
deforming forces of the extrinsic muscles of the thumb.
Surgical management
Typically CRPP with longitudinal traction and extension/abduction/pronation of the
metacarpal, as well as ulnar pressure on the base of the metacarpal.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:12 PM
AAOS | Fractures and Dislocations of the Hand and Digits
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001168
19/37

Reduction often is stabilized via percutaneous K-wire fixation from the thumb metacarpal
into the trapezium and via another wire joining the thumb and index metacarpals.
Consider ORIF (with plate and screws or screw fixation) if more than 2 to 3 mm of articular
incongruity or notable central articular impaction is present after closed reduction or if
the fracture is partially healed and closed reduction is not possible.

Proximal and Long Phalanx Fractures
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Proximal phalanx
Most transverse proximal phalanx fractures are apex palmar (Figure 6).
The central extensor tendon pulls the distal fragment dorsal, and the interossei insertion
flexes the proximal fragment.
Proximal phalanx fractures have less stability than metacarpal fractures because, dissimilar
from the metacarpals, the proximal phalanx is not supported by adjacent bones. In addition,
multiple tendon forces act on the fragments.
Cadaver model studies have estimated that shortening of the proximal phalanx produces an
extensor lag at the PIP joint, with each millimeter of bone loss equaling 12° of extensor lag;
however, the actual imbalance is variable and multifactorial.22

Most proximal phalanx base fractures are angulated apex volar.

Proximal and Long Phalanx Diaphyseal Fractures
Fractures that are not mobile and are adequately aligned are managed nonsurgically via a
brief period of immobilization followed by buddy strapping.
For mobile displaced fractures, angulation usually is apex volar because of the pull of the
central slip and the lateral bands.
Surgical management of malaligned fractures
Transverse fractures: crossed K-wires, retrograde or antegrade
Long oblique/spiral fractures: multiple screws or K-wires
Comminuted fractures: plate and screws if possible
Open fractures of the long phalanx can be managed via pinning if the PIP joint can be
mobilized (accept some DIP joint stiffness).
Plate fixation is considered for open fractures of the proximal phalanx if associated tendon
injuries place the finger at substantial risk of stiffness with K-wire fixation and
immobilization.

Epidemiology and pathoanatomy
These fractures are uncommon in adults.
In children, phalangeal neck fractures may displace and rotate 90° (apex dorsally).
With complete displacement, the volar plate may become entrapped in the fracture.

Dorsal PIP Joint Dislocations and Fracture-Dislocations
Anatomy
The accessory collateral ligaments insert onto the volar plate.
The proper collateral ligaments insert onto the condyles.
Fracture-dislocations involving more than 40% to 50% of the volar base of the joint surface
are inherently unstable.24,25
Boutonniere deformity involves compensatory hyperextension of the DIP joint (and an
inability to flex the DIP joint actively) because of tightness in the lateral bands attempting to
compensate for an inadequate central slip.
Management of PIP joint dislocations.
Most dorsal PIP joint dislocations are stable after closed reduction under a digital block, even
if a small volar plate avulsion fracture is present.
The major risk is stiffness of the PIP joint. Management consists of immediate protected
mobilization with the use of buddy straps, oval-8 splints, or self-adhesive elastic wrap and
stretching to maintain motion.
Swelling improves for 1 year; however, some increase in the diameter of the digit and joint is
expected to be permanent. Patients should be counseled that their ring size will permanently
increase one to two sizes. Stiffness and soreness may last for months and are particularly
noticeable first thing in the morning.

Displaced Unstable Transverse Distal Phalanx Fractures
Best managed via reduction and fixation with the use of K-wires or screws.
Epiphyseal Fractures (Seymour Fracture)
Open epiphyseal fractures that occur in children (typically via a crush mechanism of injury,
such as a finger getting caught in car door)
The fracture displaces through the physis dorsally and self reduces, interposing the nail bed
into the physis, which is evident on radiographs.
The interposition of germinal matrix may lead to physeal growth disruption, nonunion, nail
matrix disruption (nail plate deformity), and possibly infection.
Surgical management indicated for open injuries: Nail plate removal (blunt instruments,
hyperflexion through the fracture site), elevation of germinal matrix from the fracture site,
gentle débridement, and nail bed repair; nail bed repair typically reduces the physeal fracture,
and supplemental fixation with the use of a K-wire may be considered.27
Radiographs may be deceptive; however, the fracture most commonly is apparent with a
fracture line through the epiphysis and apex dorsal displacement of the distal portion of the
distal phalanx. Clinical examination often reveals subungual hematoma or bleeding under the
eponychial fold.

Bony or soft-tissue avulsion
Typically managed nonsurgically via DIP joint extension splinting for 6 weeks.28

advantage over nonsurgical management in most patients, regardless of displacement,
fracture size, or subluxation.29 Surgical and nonsurgical management typically result in a
bump over the dorsal aspect of the DIP joint; loss of motion; and, in the long term,
radiographic evidence of arthritis, which usually is asymptomatic.

Dorsal MCP joint dislocations are relatively uncommon. These injuries typically result

MCP joints that are hyperextended but not completely dislocated can be reduced, and a
dorsal block splint can be applied. Knowledge of the pathoanatomy is important to
prevent conversion to an irreducible complex dislocation by entrapping the volar plate.
In a simple dislocation, the volar plate is draped over the metacarpal head rather than
entrapped as it is in a complex dislocation. Traction and hyperextension may move the
entire volar plate dorsally, thereby converting to an irreducible (complex) MCP
dislocation. Instead, the wrist is flexed, and the finger is flexed without traction to
remove tension on the flexor tendons as the base of the proximal phalanx is pushed
volarly and distally to slide the displaced volar plate over the metacarpal head and back
into position.
The pathoanatomy of a complete/complex dislocation involves interposition of the
proximally avulsed volar plate between the proximal phalanx and the metacarpal head.5
Open reduction is necessary to remove the volar plate. A volar approach puts the digital
nerves at risk of injury because they are displaced into a subcutaneous position by the
prominent metacarpal head. Via a dorsal approach, a longitudinal incision, division of
the proximal aspect of the sagittal band, and division of the joint capsule expose the
metacarpal head covered by the volar plate. The volar plate is attached to the proximal
phalanx and covers the metacarpal head, blocking closed reduction. To reduce the joint,
the volar plate is split longitudinally. A Freer elevator is then used to push the ulnar and
radial aspects of the volar plate palmarly around the metacarpal head.

Nonsurgical management
Acute avulsions of the UCL of the thumb MCP joint without a Stener lesion heal sufficiently
to stabilize the joint within a few weeks.
Cast or splint immobilization for approximately 1 month is sufficient.
Surgical management
Ruptures with a Stener lesion will not heal without surgical management.
Strategies for diagnosis of a Stener lesion
Based on probability, with 30° more opening with radial stress than the opposite
uninjured side or lack of an end point5
MRI using a hand coil and special technique (incompletely tested)
Wait a few weeks and retest stability; this ligament heals quickly if a Stener lesion is not
present.
Reattach the UCL insertion to the proximal phalanx with the use of suture anchors or pull-
out suture.
In chronic settings, the ligament may not be repairable, and a graft may be necessary. If any
degenerative changes of the joint are present, arthrodesis is preferred.
RCL Disruption
Pathoanatomy
The RCL can rupture from its origin, from its insertion, or at the midsubstance.
RCL ruptures frequently are associated with dorsal or dorsoradial capsular tears and with
extensor pollicis brevis avulsions or tears. This may be appreciated on stress radiographs or
under live fluoroscopic imaging in the office, if available.
No equivalent of the Stener lesion exists; however, RCL ruptures appear more susceptible to
insufficiency and laxity.

MCP Dislocation
Pathoanatomy: the collateral ligaments and the volar plate injured
Compared with rupture of the UCL or RCL alone, healing of the ligaments is predictable with
complete dislocation; similar to PIP joint dislocation, the main risk is stiffness.
Management
Nonsurgical management
To reduce thumb MCP joint dorsal dislocations, the interphalangeal joints of the thumb and
the wrist are flexed to relax the tendons as the proximal phalanx is pushed volarly.
Traction should be avoided to prevent interposition of the soft tissues.
A few days of immobilization for comfort should suffice.
Surgical management
Similar to finger MCP dislocations, irreducible dislocations are managed via open reduction
to remove entrapped structures.
